title: Consumer choice is shifting from price alone toward perceived value, solo-life fit, concentrated trust, longevity, and AI-guided discovery
source_unit: Boston Consulting Group Center for Customer Insight, Five Consumer Behavior Shifts Reshaping Growth in 2026
geography: Consumers in 12 markets: Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Sweden, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States

denominator.unit: consumers surveyed across 12 markets, approximately more than

market_coverage.unit: percent of global population represented approximately by the 12 surveyed markets

brand_validation.unit: brands analyzed across categories and markets, approximately more than

qualitative_depth.unit: consumer qualitative interviews conducted across markets, approximately more than

five_themes.value: value over price, the longevity mindset, solo living, a new trust compass, and AI-guided decision making

observations.method: BCG Center for Customer Insight survey of more than 13,000 demographically balanced consumers in 12 markets, qualitative interviews, and analysis of more than 1,000 brands using purchase-behavior data from 2022-2026.
observations.uncertainty: The markets represent a large but non-global share of population; survey responses, stated intentions, qualitative interpretation, and proprietary brand data use different units and do not establish causal effects or future market outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Consumers across 12 markets, age and income groups, solo households, longevity-oriented consumers, AI users, brands, retailers, service providers, and category-specific audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: The five themes may partly reflect survey framing, market composition, or short-run uncertainty; traditional price sensitivity, household forms, trusted sources, and non-AI purchase journeys remain important.

denominator.unit: surveyed consumers across 12 markets, approximately more than

value_over_price.unit: percent saying they would not buy a product even when they could afford it if they did not perceive strong value

value_drivers.value: quality, convenience, service, personal connection, quantity, and trust supplement price in consumers' value judgments

brand_value_performance.unit: percent of more than 1,000 analyzed brands consistently winning on value, according to BCG's analysis

friction_cost.unit: percent saying they value products and services that reduce friction in daily life

observations.method: BCG cross-market consumer survey combined with analysis of category-specific value drivers and brand performance.
observations.uncertainty: The reported relationships describe stated perceptions and BCG's proprietary brand assessment; they do not estimate willingness-to-pay causally, identify actual household budgets, or prove that value perception predicts every purchase.
observations.subgroup: Consumers facing price pressure, convenience-sensitive shoppers, service users, category brands, retailers, and households trading money against time and effort.
observations.counterinterpretation: Price remains an important entry condition and may dominate for necessities or liquidity-constrained households; perceived value can also reflect branding, availability, or unobserved income differences.

observations.period: 2026; household form, longevity, and well-being orientation

denominator.unit: surveyed consumers across 12 markets, approximately more than

wellbeing_priority.unit: percent citing health and well-being as the number-one marker of a prosperous life, approximately three-quarters

longevity_cohort.unit: percent of consumers already embracing a longevity-oriented pursuit, approximately one-third

solo_households.unit: percent of households in mature markets consisting of a single person, approximately one in three

solo_design_gap.unit: percent of solo householders in the survey saying products and services are not designed for people like them

observations.method: BCG survey analysis of prosperity, health, longevity, household form, spending priorities, and perceived product-service fit, with contextual demographic comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The longevity and solo-living shares use different denominators and market contexts; self-reported priorities do not establish actual spending, health outcomes, household well-being, or that solo living is voluntary everywhere.
observations.subgroup: Solo householders, older consumers, longevity seekers, households purchasing health and wellness products, insurers, housing providers, food and retail categories, and care systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Living alone can reflect constraint, bereavement, migration, or housing costs as well as autonomy; health and well-being priorities can coexist with limited capacity to spend on them.

observations.period: 2026; trust and AI in consumer decision journeys

denominator.unit: surveyed consumers across 12 markets, approximately more than

information_overload.unit: percent reporting mental overwhelm from information volume

ai_purchase_use.unit: percent using AI at least occasionally in purchase journeys

ai_regular_reliance.unit: percent regularly relying on AI for purchase decisions, approximately one in five

ai_recommendation_conversion.unit: percent of AI-loyalist consumers ultimately buying products recommended by AI

trust_sources.value: experts, friends and family, and AI tools are becoming concentrated trust sources while brands do not directly control all of them

observations.method: BCG survey of consumer information use and purchase journeys, supplemented by brand and qualitative analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The AI figures are self-reported and conditional; recommendation use is not randomized exposure, and conversion does not establish product quality, consumer welfare, informed choice, privacy, or durable reliance.
observations.subgroup: AI users, information-overloaded consumers, higher-income and developing-market consumers, Gen Z and Millennials, brands, platforms, retailers, and trust intermediaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI may supplement rather than replace human advice and brand discovery; consumers can reject recommendations, and high recommendation conversion may reflect category, convenience, or selection effects.

related_sources.claim: BCG's related consumer-AI work provides a complementary route on exposure and resilience at the interface.
BCG's related consumer-goods analysis provides complementary firm and retail context for AI-mediated demand.

boundary: This record adds a publication-level consumer route across perceived value, price, time and convenience, solo living, longevity, trust, information overload, and AI-guided purchase discovery. It uses BCG's aggregate survey, interviews, and proprietary brand analysis, not individual purchase histories, household budgets, respondent-level psychological profiles, causal AI effects, welfare estimates, or proof that these themes apply uniformly across consumers or markets.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official BCG publication page reviewed for the 12-market sample, 13,000-plus consumers, 1,000-plus brands, five themes, value-over-price, longevity, solo living, trust, information overload, and AI purchase figures.
